claims.text: Prior systematic review identified only five mental health apps that were supported by trial-based evidence from randomized controlled trials.
Computerized cognitive behavioral therapy (CCBT) for depression and anxiety yields a medium effect size of g = 0.77 across 49 randomized controlled trials.
Computerized cognitive behavioral therapy yields an effect size of g = 0.88 across a meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials.
Including homework or between-session activities in therapy produces an effect size of d = 0.48 compared to therapy without homework.
Transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral therapy yields a standardized mean difference of -0.79 across different anxiety disorders.
Exercise interventions for individuals diagnosed with mental illness produce a standardized mean difference of 0.80 for depressive symptoms.
Behavioral activation for clinical depression outperforms control conditions with a standardized mean difference of -0.70.
Relaxation training demonstrates an effect size of d = 0.57 for reducing anxiety across 27 randomized controlled trials.
Electronic-game-based depression interventions demonstrate a moderate effect size of d = -0.47 on depressive symptoms across 10 randomized controlled trials.
A set of 16 evidence-based recommendations guides the design, functionality, and evaluation of future mental health smartphone apps.

evidence.description: Their systematic review identified only 5 apps that had supporting evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
A meta-analysis of 49 RCTs revealed a significant medium effect size (g = 0.77, 95% CI 0.59-0.95) for computerized CBT (CCBT) for depression and anxiety.
Another meta-analysis of 22 RCTs found an even greater effect size (g = 0.88, 95% CI 0.76-0.99).
A meta-analysis of studies that compared therapy with and without homework found an effect size of d = 0.48 in favor of using between-session activities.
A meta-analysis of RCTs found a large effect size (standardized mean difference = −0.79, 95% CI −1.30 to −0.27) for TCBT across different anxiety disorders.

A meta-analysis of 39 RCTs examined the effects of exercise on people diagnosed with a mental illness, and found large effect sizes for depressive symptoms (standardized mean difference = 0.80, 95% CI 0.47-1.13).
A meta-analysis of 17 RCTs reported that BA for clinical depression outperformed control conditions (standardized mean difference = −0.70, 95% CI −1.00 to −0.39).
A meta-analysis of 27 RCTs found a medium to large effect size for relaxation training on anxiety (d = 0.57, 95% CI 0.52-0.68).
A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs found that electronic-game-based depression interventions had a moderate effect on depressive symptoms (d = −0.47, 95% CI −0.69 to −0.24).
Sixteen recommendations were formulated based on literature across mental health interventions, preventative health, mobile health, and mobile app design.

methodologies.name: Literature Review and Recommendation Framework Synthesis
methodologies.description: A cross-disciplinary literature review across mental health interventions, mobile health, and app design to formulate 16 practical, evidence-based recommendations for mental health app development.
conditions: Peer-reviewed articles published between March 1975 and March 2015
Directly relevant to mental health or computerized health interventions

limitations.text: The recommendations presented in this review have not been rigorously validated by RCTs specifically in a mental health smartphone app setting.
The study was not a systematic review, so the specific number of articles found and excluded during searches was not tracked.
Many currently available mental health apps lack features that would improve functionality or include non-optimized features.
Developers of mental health apps rarely conduct or publish trial-based experimental validation of their applications.
None of the five mental health apps previously validated by RCTs in systematic review remained available to consumers on app stores.

future_work.text: Conduct randomized controlled trials to validate future mental health apps, their design principles, and the specific 16 recommendations presented in this review.
Develop a well-validated, standardized, and brief assessment tool for mental health literacy suitable for administration on smartphone interfaces.
Investigate the relative efficacy of reflection-focused, education-focused, and goal-focused mental health app designs across different user populations.
